nodes.statement: The proof is the same as that of \cref{prop:escape_3M} and we just present the sketch. We first show the following claim: \begin{claim}[Concentration of the variance for the Best-of-two] Consider the Best-of-two on $G(2n,p,q)$ that is both $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_1$-good and $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_2$-good. Then, two constants $C_1,C_2>0$ exist such that \begin{align*} &\forall A\subseteq V, \, \forall i\in\{1,2\}\,: \\ &\hspace{3em} \left|\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}\left[|A'_i|\,\middle|\, A \right] - |A_i| g_1\left(\frac{|A_i|p+|A_{3-i}|q}{n(p+q)}\right) - (n-|A_i|) g_2\left(\frac{|A_i|p+|A_{3-i}|q}{n(p+q)}\right) \right| \leq C_2\sqrt{\frac{n}{p}}, \end{align*} where $g_i(x)\mathrel{\mathop:}= f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_i(x)(1-f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_i(x))$ for $i=1,2$. \end{claim} \begin{proof} That variance $\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[|A'_i| \mid A]$ can be represented as \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[|A'_i| \mid A] = \sum_{v\in V_i} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[v\in A'](1-\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[v\in A']) = \sum_{v\in A_i} g_1\left(\frac{\deg_A(v)}{\deg(v)}\right) + \sum_{v\in V_i\setminus A_i} g_2\left(\frac{\deg_A(v)}{\deg(v)}\right). \end{align*} Therefore, \cref{claim:mainthm_Var_2C} immediately follows from the property~\ref{pro:gomiN} and \cref{thm:fgood}. \end{proof} From \cref{claim:mainthm_Var_2C}, we have $\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[\alpha'_i\mid A]=\Omega(n^{-1})$ if $\min\{\alpha_1,1-\alpha_1,\alpha_2,1-\alpha_2\}=\Omega(1)$. This verifies the condition~\ref{asm:asm2} of Assumption~\ref{asm:escape_assumption0}. We consider two cases: $u\neq \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ and $u=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. Suppose that $u\neq\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. Then both $\mathbf{d}^*_1$ and $\mathbf{d}^*_2$ satisfy Assumption~\ref{asm:escape_assumption2} and we can apply \cref{prop:escape}. Suppose that $u=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. In this case, we have $\mathbf{d}^*_1=\mathbf{d}^*_2=(0,0)$. This point satisfies conditions~\ref{asm:asm4} and \ref{asm:asm5} of Assumption~\ref{asm:escape_assumption1} and apply \cref{prop:escape}.
nodes.statement_short: Mirror the Best-of-three escape proof: a variance bound (Claim 10.6) gives (A2); then apply Proposition 7.8 under Assumption 7.7, or 7.6 at the degenerate $u=(\sqrt5-1)/2$.

nodes.name: Variance claim
nodes.statement: The proof is the same as that of \cref{prop:escape_3M} and we just present the sketch. We first show the following claim: \begin{claim}[Concentration of the variance for the Best-of-two] Consider the Best-of-two on $G(2n,p,q)$ that is both $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_1$-good and $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_2$-good. Then, two constants $C_1,C_2>0$ exist such that \begin{align*} &\forall A\subseteq V, \, \forall i\in\{1,2\}\,: \\ &\hspace{3em} \left|\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}\left[|A'_i|\,\middle|\, A \right] - |A_i| g_1\left(\frac{|A_i|p+|A_{3-i}|q}{n(p+q)}\right) - (n-|A_i|) g_2\left(\frac{|A_i|p+|A_{3-i}|q}{n(p+q)}\right) \right| \leq C_2\sqrt{\frac{n}{p}}, \end{align*} where $g_i(x)\mathrel{\mathop:}= f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_i(x)(1-f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_i(x))$ for $i=1,2$. \end{claim} \begin{proof} That variance $\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[|A'_i| \mid A]$ can be represented as \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[|A'_i| \mid A] = \sum_{v\in V_i} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[v\in A'](1-\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[v\in A']) = \sum_{v\in A_i} g_1\left(\frac{\deg_A(v)}{\deg(v)}\right) + \sum_{v\in V_i\setminus A_i} g_2\left(\frac{\deg_A(v)}{\deg(v)}\right). \end{align*} Therefore, \cref{claim:mainthm_Var_2C} immediately follows from the property~\ref{pro:gomiN} and \cref{thm:fgood}. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Concentration of the variance for the Best-of-two
nodes.statement: Consider the Best-of-two on $G(2n,p,q)$ that is both $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_1$-good and $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_2$-good. Then, two constants $C_1,C_2>0$ exist such that \begin{align*} &\forall A\subseteq V, \, \forall i\in\{1,2\}\,: \\ &\hspace{3em} \left|\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}\left[|A'_i|\,\middle|\, A \right] - |A_i| g_1\left(\frac{|A_i|p+|A_{3-i}|q}{n(p+q)}\right) - (n-|A_i|) g_2\left(\frac{|A_i|p+|A_{3-i}|q}{n(p+q)}\right) \right| \leq C_2\sqrt{\frac{n}{p}}, \end{align*} where $g_i(x)\mathrel{\mathop:}= f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_i(x)(1-f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_i(x))$ for $i=1,2$.
assumptions: Consider the Best-of-two on $G(2n,p,q)$ that is both $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_1$-good and $f^{\mathrm{Bo2}}_2$-good.
conclusions: two constants $C_1,C_2>0$ exist such that
nodes.label: claim:mainthm_Var_2C

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 10.6
nodes.statement: That variance $\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[|A'_i| \mid A]$ can be represented as \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[|A'_i| \mid A] = \sum_{v\in V_i} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[v\in A'](1-\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[v\in A']) = \sum_{v\in A_i} g_1\left(\frac{\deg_A(v)}{\deg(v)}\right) + \sum_{v\in V_i\setminus A_i} g_2\left(\frac{\deg_A(v)}{\deg(v)}\right). \end{align*} Therefore, \cref{claim:mainthm_Var_2C} immediately follows from the property~\ref{pro:gomiN} and \cref{thm:fgood}.
nodes.statement_short: Write the variance as sums of $g_i(\deg_A(v)/\deg(v))$ and apply (P2).

nodes.name: (A2)
nodes.statement: From \cref{claim:mainthm_Var_2C}, we have $\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[\alpha'_i\mid A]=\Omega(n^{-1})$ if $\min\{\alpha_1,1-\alpha_1,\alpha_2,1-\alpha_2\}=\Omega(1)$. This verifies the condition~\ref{asm:asm2} of Assumption~\ref{asm:escape_assumption0}.

nodes.name: Generic $u$
nodes.statement: We consider two cases: $u\neq \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ and $u=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. Suppose that $u\neq\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. Then both $\mathbf{d}^*_1$ and $\mathbf{d}^*_2$ satisfy Assumption~\ref{asm:escape_assumption2} and we can apply \cref{prop:escape}.

nodes.name: Degenerate $u$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $u=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$. In this case, we have $\mathbf{d}^*_1=\mathbf{d}^*_2=(0,0)$. This point satisfies conditions~\ref{asm:asm4} and \ref{asm:asm5} of Assumption~\ref{asm:escape_assumption1} and apply \cref{prop:escape}.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorems 1.3 and 1.5
nodes.statement: Combining \cref{prop:2Cvectorfield,prop:sink_2C,prop:fastconsensus_2C,prop:escape_2C}, the proofs of \cref{thm:phasetransition_2C,thm:worst_case_2C} follow from the same argument as that of \cref{thm:phasetransition_3M,thm:worst_case_3M} (see \cref{sec:apply_to_3M}).
nodes.statement_short: Same argument as for Theorems 1.2 and 1.4, using the Best-of-two Propositions 10.2-10.5.

nodes.name: Probability of reaching sink areas
nodes.statement: For an application to distributed community detection algorithms, it is significant to estimate the probability that the voting process reaches the sink areas (in particular, starting from the source area). This is a possible future direction of this paper.
also_stated_at: To estimate the probability which the process reaches sink areas from the source area is future work to consider an application of these processes to distributed community detection algorithms.

nodes.name: Best-of-$(2k+1)$ as a polynomial voting process
nodes.statement: For example, consider the Best-of-$(2k+1)$ voting process for a positive constant $k$. This process is defined by $f_1(x)=f_2(x)\mathrel{\mathop:}= \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[{\rm Bin}(2k+1,x)\geq k+1]=\sum_{i=k+1}^{2k+1}\binom{2k+1}{i}x^i(1-x)^{2k+1-i}$. \Cref{thm:approximation_vectorfield_general} guarantees $\|{\boldsymbol \alpha}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_\infty\leq C^t(\sqrt{1/np}+\sqrt{\log n/n})$ for this process.
nodes.statement_short: Best-of-$(2k+1)$ is polynomial voting with $f_1=f_2=\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(2k+1,x)\ge k+1]$, so Theorem 6.2 applies.

nodes.name: Extension to multi-community, multi-opinion SBMs
nodes.statement: Moreover, using \cref{lem:WIdiscrepancy}, it is not difficult to extend \cref{thm:approximation_vectorfield_general} to voting processes on general stochastic block models that has $c_1$ communities each of size $\Omega(n)$ and initially involving $c_2$ opinions, where $c_1, c_2$ denote arbitrary positive constants. This setting yields induced dynamical systems of dimension more than two.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 8.1 extends Theorem 6.2 to SBMs with $c_1$ communities and $c_2$ opinions, giving higher-dimensional induced systems.

nodes.name: Zero areas and convergence of higher-dimensional induced systems
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, it may not be easy to specify other properties (e.g.~zero areas, convergence properties, \ldots) of $(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})_{t\in \mathbbm{N}}$ corresponding to such processes. This problem is left for future work.

nodes.name: Worst-case consensus time on sparse random graphs
nodes.statement: Also, the worst-case analysis of the consensus time for sparse random graphs remains open in this paper.

nodes.name: Singular value
nodes.statement: For a real matrix $A\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, \emph{singular values} $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ of $A$ are nonnegative square roots of eigenvalues of $AA^\top$. We write $\sigma_i(A)$ when we specify $A$. In particular, \emph{the maximum singular value}, denoted by $\sigma_{\max}$, is the largest value among all singular values.
nodes.genus: nonnegative square roots of eigenvalues of $AA^\top$

nodes.name: Variational characterization of $\sigma_{\max}$
nodes.statement: For a real matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, it holds that \begin{align*} \sigma_{\max}=\max_{\mathbf{v}\in \mathbb{R}^n:\|\mathbf{v}\|_2=1}\|A\mathbf{v}\|_2, \end{align*} where the norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the $\ell^2$ norm. In particular, it holds that \begin{align*} \|A\mathbf{v}\|_2\leq \sigma_{\max}\|\mathbf{v}\|_2 \end{align*} for any vector $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.label: prop:singularvalue

nodes.name: Inverse Function Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a continuously differentiable function from an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ into $\mathbb{R}^k$. Suppose that the Jacobian matrix $J$ at $\mathbf{p}\in U$ is invertible. Then there is a neighborhood $V$ of $\mathbf{p}$ such that the restriction of $f$ to $V$ is invertible. Moreover, the Jacobian matrix of $f^{-1}$ at $p$ is given by $J^{-1}$.
nodes.label: thm:IFT

nodes.name: Lipschitz condition
nodes.statement: Consider a function $H:S\to T$, where $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m$ and $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ are closed sets. The function $H$ satisfies the \emph{Lipschitz condition} if there exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that \begin{align*} \|H(\mathbf{x})-H(\mathbf{y})\|_\infty \leq C\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_\infty \end{align*} holds for any $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S$.
nodes.label: def:lipschitzdef

nodes.name: Lipschitz bound via maximal singular value of the Jacobian
nodes.statement: Let $O\subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be an open set and $S\subseteq O$ be a compact convex subset of $O$. Suppose that $H:O\to \mathbb{R}^k$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $O$. Then $H$ is Lipschitz continuous on $C$ and \begin{align*} \|H(\mathbf{x})-H(\mathbf{y})\|_\infty \leq \max_{\mathbf{p}\in S}\sigma_{\max}(J_{\mathbf{p}})\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_\infty, \end{align*} where $J_{\mathbf{p}}$ is the Jacobian matrix at $\mathbf{p}$.
nodes.label: prop:lipschitzC1prop

nodes.name: Polynomial maps are Lipschitz on the cube
nodes.statement: Let $H:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a function given by \begin{align*} H(\mathbf{x})=(H_1(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,H_n(\mathbf{x})), \end{align*} where $H_i(\mathbf{x})=H_i(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ is a polynomial on $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ for all $i\in[n]$. Then, $H$ satisfies the Lipschitz condition on $[0,1]^m$.
assumptions: where $H_i(\mathbf{x})=H_i(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ is a polynomial on $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ for all $i\in[n]$.
conclusions: Then, $H$ satisfies the Lipschitz condition on $[0,1]^m$.
nodes.label: cor:lipschitzprop

nodes.name: Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be independent random variables taking values in $[0,1]$. Let $X=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. Then the following hold: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)] \item for any $\delta\geq 0$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X\geq (1+\delta)\mathbf{E}[X]] \leq \exp\left(-\frac{\min\{\delta,\delta^2\}\mathbf{E}[X]}{3}\right). \end{align*} \item for any $\delta\in [0,1]$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X\leq (1-\delta)\mathbf{E}[X]] \leq \exp\left(-\frac{\delta^2\mathbf{E}[X]}{2}\right). \end{align*} \item for any $k\geq 2\mathrm{e}\mathbf{E}[X]$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[X\geq k \right]\leq 2^{-k}. \end{align*} Here, $\mathrm{e}$ denotes the Napier constant. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:chernoff

nodes.name: Additive Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: \ \noindent Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be independent random variables taking values in $[0,1]$. Let $X=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. Then for any $\delta \geq 0$, \begin{align*} &\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X\geq \mathbf{E}[X]+\delta]\leq \exp\left(-\frac{1}{3}\min\left\{\frac{\delta^2}{\mathbf{E}[X]},\delta\right\}\right), \\ &\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X\leq \mathbf{E}[X]-\delta]\leq \exp\left(-\frac{\delta^2}{2\mathbf{E}[X]}\right). \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:chernoff-additive

nodes.name: Hoeffding bound
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be independent random variables. Assume that each $X_i$ takes values in a real interval $[a_i, b_i]$ of length $c_i\mathrel{\mathop:}= b_i-a_i$. Let $X=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. Then for any $\delta>0$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[X\geq \mathbf{E}[X]+\delta \right]&\leq \exp\left(-\frac{2\delta^2 }{\sum_{i=1}^nc_i^2}\right), \\ \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[X\leq \mathbf{E}[X]-\delta \right]&\leq \exp\left(-\frac{2\delta^2 }{\sum_{i=1}^nc_i^2}\right). \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:Hoeffding

nodes.name: Berry-Esseen theorem
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be independent random variables such that $\mathbf{E}[X_i]=0$, $\mathbf{E}[X_i^2]>0$, $\mathbf{E}[|X_i|^3]<\infty$ for all $i\in [n]$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{E}[X_i^2]=1$. Let $X=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$ and let $\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^x\mathrm{e}^{-y^2/2}\mathrm{d}y$ (the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution). Then \begin{align*} \sup_{x\in \mathbbm{R}}\bigl|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[X\leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\bigr| &\leq 5.6 \sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{E}[|X_i|^3]. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:Berry-Esseen

nodes.name: Berry-Esseen bound for bounded summands
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ be $n$ independent random variables such that $\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]\neq 0$ and $|X_i-\mathbf{E}[X_i]|\leq C<\infty$ for all $i\in [n]$ where $X=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. Then for any $x\in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{align*} \left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\frac{X-\mathbf{E}[X]}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}}\leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right| &\leq \frac{5.6C}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Normalized sums of independent bounded variables are within $5.6C/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}X}$ of the standard normal CDF.
nodes.label: cor:BEbound_cor

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary A.11
nodes.statement: For all $i\in [n]$, let \begin{align*} Z_i&\mathrel{\mathop:}= \frac{X_i-\mathbf{E}[X_i]}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}}, \\ Z&\mathrel{\mathop:}= \sum_{\substack{i\in [n]: \mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0}}Z_i =\sum_{i\in [n]}Z_i. \end{align*} Note that $\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]=0 \iff \sum_{z}z^2\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[Z_i=z]=0 \iff \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[Z_i=0]=1$. Then, for all $i\in \{j\in [n]: \mathbf{E}[Z_j^2]> 0\}$, it is easy to check that $\mathbf{E}[Z_i]=0$, $\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0$, and $\mathbf{E}[|Z_i|^3]\leq \frac{C^3}{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]^{3/2}}<\infty$. Furthermore, \begin{align*} \sum_{\substack{i\in [n]:\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0}}\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2] &=\sum_{i\in [n]}\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2] =\frac{\sum_{i\in [n]}\mathbf{E}[(X_i-\mathbf{E}[X_i])^2]}{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}=1. \end{align*} Thus we can apply \cref{lem:Berry-Esseen} to $Z$ and it holds that \begin{align*} \left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\frac{X-\mathbf{E}[X]}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}} \leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right| &=\left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right|\\ &=\left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[Z \leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right|\\ &\leq 5.6 \sum_{i\in[n]:\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0}\mathbf{E}[|Z_i|^3]\\ &\leq \frac{5.6C}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}} \sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2] =\frac{5.6C}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the summands and apply Berry-Esseen, bounding third moments by $C$ times second moments.

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: For all $i\in [n]$, let \begin{align*} Z_i&\mathrel{\mathop:}= \frac{X_i-\mathbf{E}[X_i]}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}}, \\ Z&\mathrel{\mathop:}= \sum_{\substack{i\in [n]: \mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0}}Z_i =\sum_{i\in [n]}Z_i. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Check hypotheses
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]=0 \iff \sum_{z}z^2\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[Z_i=z]=0 \iff \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[Z_i=0]=1$. Then, for all $i\in \{j\in [n]: \mathbf{E}[Z_j^2]> 0\}$, it is easy to check that $\mathbf{E}[Z_i]=0$, $\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0$, and $\mathbf{E}[|Z_i|^3]\leq \frac{C^3}{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]^{3/2}}<\infty$. Furthermore, \begin{align*} \sum_{\substack{i\in [n]:\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0}}\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2] &=\sum_{i\in [n]}\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2] =\frac{\sum_{i\in [n]}\mathbf{E}[(X_i-\mathbf{E}[X_i])^2]}{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}=1. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Apply Berry-Esseen
nodes.statement: Thus we can apply \cref{lem:Berry-Esseen} to $Z$ and it holds that \begin{align*} \left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\frac{X-\mathbf{E}[X]}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}} \leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right| &=\left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right|\\ &=\left|\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[Z \leq x\right]-\Phi(x)\right|\\ &\leq 5.6 \sum_{i\in[n]:\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2]>0}\mathbf{E}[|Z_i|^3]\\ &\leq \frac{5.6C}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}} \sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{E}[Z_i^2] =\frac{5.6C}{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbf{Var}}[X]}}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Drift lemma for escaping $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ (Lemma 4.5 of AMLEFG18)
nodes.statement: Consider a Markov chain $(X_t)_{t=1}^\infty$ with finite state space $\Omega$ and a function $f:\Omega \to \{0,\ldots,n\}$. Let $C_3$ be arbitrary constant and $m=C_3 \sqrt{n\log n}$. Suppose that $\Omega,f$ and $m$ satisfies the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}[label=$(\arabic*)$] \item For any positive constant $h$, there exists a positive constant $C_1<1$ such that \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[f(X_{t+1})<h\sqrt{n}\,\middle|\,f(X_t)\leq m\right] < C_1. \end{align*} \item Three positive constants $\epsilon, C_2$ and $h$ exist such that, for any $x\in \Omega$ satisfying $h\sqrt{n}\leq f(x)<m$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[f(X_{t+1})< (1+\epsilon)f(X_t) \,\middle|\, X_t=x\right] < \exp\left(-C_2\frac{f(x)^2}{n}\right). \end{align*} \end{enumerate} Then $f(X_\tau) \geq m$ holds for some $\tau=O(\log n)$.
nodes.label: lem:nazolemma

nodes.name: Drift corollary restricted to a set $\mathcal{B}$
nodes.statement: Consider a Markov chain $(X_t)_{t=1}^\infty$ with finite state space $\Omega$ and a function $f:\Omega \to \{0,\ldots,n\}$. Let $C_3$ be arbitrary constant and $m=C_3 \sqrt{n\log n}$. Consider a set $\mathcal{B}\subseteq \Omega$ such that \begin{align*} \mathcal{B}\subseteq \{x\in \Omega\,:\,f(x)< m\}. \end{align*} Suppose that $\Omega,f,m$ and $\mathcal{B}$ satisfy the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}[label=$(\arabic*')$] \item For any positive constant $h$, there exists a positive constant $C_1<1$ such that \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[f(X_{t+1})<h\sqrt{n}\,\middle|\,f(X_t)\leq m,X_t\in\mathcal{B}\right] < C_1. \end{align*} \item Three positive constants $\epsilon, C_2,h$ exist such that, for any $x\in \mathcal{B}$ satisfying $h\sqrt{n}\leq f(x)<m$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[f(X_{t+1})< (1+\epsilon)f(X_t) \,\middle|\, X_t=x\right] < \exp\left(-C_2\frac{f(x)^2}{n}\right). \end{align*} \item For some constant $C_4>0$, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[X_{t+1}\not\in\mathcal{B}\text{ and } f(X_{t+1})< m\,\middle|\,X_t\in\mathcal{B}\right] \leq O(n^{-C_2}). \end{align*} \end{enumerate} Then, \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[f(X_\tau) \geq m \mid X_0\in \mathcal{B}\right]\geq 1-n^{-\Omega(1)} \end{align*} holds for some $\tau=O(\log n)$.
nodes.statement_short: If within $\mathcal B$ the potential $f$ escapes $O(\sqrt n)$ with constant probability and grows multiplicatively, and leaving $\mathcal B$ otherwise is unlikely, then $f\ge m$ within $O(\log n)$ steps w.h.p.
nodes.label: cor:nazocor

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary A.13
nodes.statement_short: Couple with a chain on $\mathcal B$ plus two absorbing states and apply Lemma A.12; the bad absorbing state is reached with probability $n^{-\Omega(1)}$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary chain
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega'=\mathcal{B}\cup \{a,b\}$ be the state space with two special states $a$ and $b$. We consider a Markov chain $(X'_t)_{t+1}^\infty$ on $\Omega'$ by \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X'_{t+1}=x \mid X'_t=y] =\begin{cases} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X_{t+1}=x \mid X_t=y] & \text{if $x,y\in \mathcal{B}$},\\ \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X_{t+1}\not\in\mathcal{B}\land f(X_{t+1})< m \mid X_t=y] & \text{if $x=a$ and $y\in\mathcal{B}$}, \\ \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[f(X_{t+1})\geq m \mid X_t=y] &\text{if $x=b$ and $y\in\mathcal{B}$}, \\ 1 & \text{if $x=y\in\{a,b\}$}. \end{cases} \end{align*} In other words, the special state $a$ corresponds to the event ``$f(x)<m$ and $x\not\in\mathcal{B}$~", and $b$ does ``$f(x)\geq m$".

nodes.name: Coupling
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X'_0\in \mathcal{B}$ and let $\tau'=\min\{t:X'_t\not\in\mathcal{B}\}>0$ be the stopping time. Then, the above definition of $X'_t$ naturally yields a coupling $(X_t,X'_t)_{t<\tau'}$ satisfying $X_t=X'_t$ for $t<\tau'$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma A.12
nodes.statement: Let $f':\Omega'\to\{0,\ldots,n\}$ be a function given by \begin{align*} f'(x) = \begin{cases} f(x) & \text{if $x\in\mathcal{B}$},\\ n & \text{if $x\in \{a,b\}$}. \end{cases} \end{align*} Then, the Markov chain $(X'_t)$ on $\Omega'$ and the function $f'$ satisfies the conditions \ref{state:nazo_sqrt} and \ref{state:nazo_cher} of \cref{lem:nazolemma}. Hence, for some $\tau=O(\log n)$, it holds that $X'_\tau \in \{a,b\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The chain reaches $\{a,b\}$ in $O(\log n)$ steps.

nodes.name: Absorbed at $b$
nodes.statement: We insist that $X'_\tau=b$, that is, $f(X_\tau)\geq m$. Indeed, from the condition~\ref{cond:whp}, we have \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[X'_\tau=a \mid X'_0\in\mathcal{B}]&\leq \tau\cdot O(n^{-c_2}) \\ &\leq n^{-\Omega(1)}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Monotone increasing function
nodes.statement: We say a function $f:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb{R}$ is \emph{monotone increasing} if $f(\mathbf{x})\leq f(\mathbf{y})$ whenever $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_M),\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_M)\in\{0,1\}^M$ satisfies $x_i\leq y_i$ for every $i=1,\ldots,M$.

nodes.name: FKG inequality
nodes.statement: For a given set $[M]=\{1,2, \ldots, M\}$, let $I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_M$ be independent binary random variables. Then for any two monotone increase functions $f,g: \{0,1\}^{M}\to \mathbb{R}$, it holds that \begin{align*} \mathbf{E}[f(\mathbf{I})g(\mathbf{I})]&\geq \mathbf{E}[f(\mathbf{I})]\mathbf{E}[g(\mathbf{I})] \end{align*} where $\mathbf{I}=(I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_M)\in \{0,1\}^{M}$.
nodes.label: lem:FKG

nodes.name: Janson's inequality
nodes.label: lem:Janson

nodes.name: Kim-Vu concentration inequality
nodes.statement: For a given set $[M]=\{1,2, \ldots, M\}$, let $I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_M$ be independent binary random variables. Now, let $\mathcal{E}\subseteq 2^{[M]}$ be a collection of subsets of $[M]$ ($F\subseteq [M]$ for all $F\in \mathcal{E}$) and let \begin{align*} Y=\sum_{F\in \mathcal{E}}w(F)\prod_{e\in F}I_e, \end{align*} where $w(F)$ are positive coefficients. For a subset $A\subseteq [M]$, define $Y_{A}$ as \begin{align*} Y_{A}=\sum_{\substack{F\in\mathcal{E}:\\F\supseteq A}} w(F)\prod_{e\in F\setminus A}I_e. \end{align*} If the polynomial $Y$ has degree at most $k$ (i.e.~$\max_{F\in\mathcal{E}}|F|\leq k$), then for any positive $\lambda>1$, it holds that \begin{align*} \mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[|Y-\mathbf{E}[Y]|\geq \sqrt{k! \max_{A\subseteq [M]}\mathbf{E}[Y_{A}]\max_{A\subseteq [M]:A\neq \emptyset}\mathbf{E}[Y_{A}]}(8\lambda)^k\right]\leq 2\exp(2+(k-1)\log M-\lambda). \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:Kim-Vu

nodes.name: Order $\leq_K$
nodes.statement: For two points $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)$ and $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2)$, we write $\mathbf{x}\leq_K \mathbf{y}$ if both $x_1\leq y_1$ and $y_2 \leq x_2$ hold.

nodes.name: Competitive map
nodes.statement: For $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, a map $T:S \to S$ is \emph{competitive} if $T$ is monotone with respect to the relation $\leq_K$ (i.e.~$T(\mathbf{x})\leq_K T(\mathbf{y})$ whenever $\mathbf{x}\leq_K \mathbf{y}$).
differentia: $T$ is monotone with respect to the relation $\leq_K$

nodes.name: Componentwise order $\leq$
nodes.statement: We use $\mathbf{x}\leq \mathbf{y}$ for the usual component-wise comparison (i.e.~$\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{y}$ if $x_i\leq y_i$ for $i=1,2$).

nodes.name: Conditions (C1)-(C4) on the map $T$
nodes.statement: Throughout this section, we let \begin{align*} S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x\geq 0,y\geq 0,x+y\leq 1\} \end{align*} and our map $T:S\to S$ is supposed to satisfy the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}[label=(C\arabic*)] \item $T$ is competitive. \item $T$ is injective. \item $T$ is $C^1$. \item The inverse map $T^{-1}$ is monotone with respective to the ordinal relation $\leq$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: On the simplex $S$, $T$ is competitive, injective, $C^1$, with monotone inverse.

nodes.name: Fixed point
nodes.statement: A point $\mathbf{x}$ is a \emph{fixed point} if $T(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}$.

nodes.name: Orbit convergence for competitive maps satisfying (C1)-(C4)
nodes.statement: Suppose that a map $T:S\to S$ satisfies the conditions \ref{cond:map_condition1} to \ref{cond:map_condition4}. Then, for any point $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}T^n(\mathbf{x})$ exists and the limit is a fixed point of $T$.
assumptions: Suppose that a map $T:S\to S$ satisfies the conditions \ref{cond:map_condition1} to \ref{cond:map_condition4}.
conclusions: for any point $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}T^n(\mathbf{x})$ exists and the limit is a fixed point of $T$
nodes.label: thm:orbit_convergence

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A.17
nodes.statement: For two points $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)$ and $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2)$, we write $\mathbf{x}\ll \mathbf{y}$ if $x_1<y_1$ and $x_2<y_2$. We use the following known result: \begin{theorem}[Theorem 5.28 of \cite{HS05}] Suppose that a competitive map $T:S\to S$ satisfies the following: \begin{center} $\mathbf{x}\leq \mathbf{y}$ for any $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S$ of $T(\mathbf{x}) \ll T(\mathbf{y})$. \end{center} Then, for any $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the sequence $(T^n(\mathbf{x}))_{n\geq 0}$ converges to some fixed point of $T$ \end{theorem} For any points $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S$ of $T(\mathbf{x}) \ll T(\mathbf{y})$, the conditions \ref{cond:map_condition2} and \ref{cond:map_condition4} yield that $\mathbf{x}=T^{-1}(T(\mathbf{x})) \leq T^{-1}(T(\mathbf{y})) = \mathbf{y}$. Therefore, we can directly apply \cref{thm:competitive_map_known_result}.
nodes.statement_short: (C2) and (C4) give the order condition of Hirsch-Smith Theorem 5.28, which yields convergence.

nodes.name: Known result
nodes.statement: For two points $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)$ and $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2)$, we write $\mathbf{x}\ll \mathbf{y}$ if $x_1<y_1$ and $x_2<y_2$. We use the following known result: \begin{theorem}[Theorem 5.28 of \cite{HS05}] Suppose that a competitive map $T:S\to S$ satisfies the following: \begin{center} $\mathbf{x}\leq \mathbf{y}$ for any $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S$ of $T(\mathbf{x}) \ll T(\mathbf{y})$. \end{center} Then, for any $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the sequence $(T^n(\mathbf{x}))_{n\geq 0}$ converges to some fixed point of $T$ \end{theorem}

nodes.name: Convergence of competitive maps (Hirsch-Smith Thm 5.28)
nodes.statement: Suppose that a competitive map $T:S\to S$ satisfies the following: \begin{center} $\mathbf{x}\leq \mathbf{y}$ for any $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S$ of $T(\mathbf{x}) \ll T(\mathbf{y})$. \end{center} Then, for any $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the sequence $(T^n(\mathbf{x}))_{n\geq 0}$ converges to some fixed point of $T$
nodes.label: thm:competitive_map_known_result

nodes.name: Verify and apply
nodes.statement: For any points $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S$ of $T(\mathbf{x}) \ll T(\mathbf{y})$, the conditions \ref{cond:map_condition2} and \ref{cond:map_condition4} yield that $\mathbf{x}=T^{-1}(T(\mathbf{x})) \leq T^{-1}(T(\mathbf{y})) = \mathbf{y}$. Therefore, we can directly apply \cref{thm:competitive_map_known_result}.
nodes.statement_short: (C2),(C4) give the hypothesis; apply Theorem A.18.

nodes.name: Jacobian sign criterion for competitiveness
nodes.statement: A map $T:S\to S$ is competitive if, for any point $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the Jacobian matrix $J$ at $\mathbf{x}$ is of the form \begin{align*} J=\left(\begin{array}{cc} j_{11} & j_{12} \\ j_{21} & j_{22} \end{array} \right) \end{align*} with $j_{11},j_{22}\geq 0$ and $j_{12},j_{21}\leq 0$.
assumptions: for any point $\mathbf{x}\in S$, the Jacobian matrix $J$ at $\mathbf{x}$ is of the form
conclusions: A map $T:S\to S$ is competitive
nodes.label: lem:criterion_C1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.19
nodes.statement: Let $T(\mathbf{x})=(T_1(\mathbf{x}),T_2(\mathbf{x}))$ for $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)\in S$. From the assumption on the Jacobian matrix, the function $T_i$ is nondecreasing on $x_i$ and is nonincreasing on $x_{3-i}$. With this in mind, for any $(a,b),\,(c,d)\in S$ of $(a,b)\leq_K (c,d)$, we have \begin{align*} &T_1(a,b) \leq T_1(c,b) \leq T_1(c,d),\\ &T_2(a,b) \geq T_2(a,d) \geq T_2(c,d). \end{align*} In other words, $T(a,b)\leq_K T(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sign pattern makes $T_i$ nondecreasing in $x_i$ and nonincreasing in $x_{3-i}$; chain the inequalities.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of components
nodes.statement: Let $T(\mathbf{x})=(T_1(\mathbf{x}),T_2(\mathbf{x}))$ for $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)\in S$. From the assumption on the Jacobian matrix, the function $T_i$ is nondecreasing on $x_i$ and is nonincreasing on $x_{3-i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Read monotonicity of $T_i$ from the Jacobian.

nodes.name: Chain inequalities
nodes.statement: With this in mind, for any $(a,b),\,(c,d)\in S$ of $(a,b)\leq_K (c,d)$, we have \begin{align*} &T_1(a,b) \leq T_1(c,b) \leq T_1(c,d),\\ &T_2(a,b) \geq T_2(a,d) \geq T_2(c,d). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In other words, $T(a,b)\leq_K T(c,d)$.

nodes.name: Determinant criterion for (C4)
nodes.statement: Suppose that a map $T:S\to S$ satisfies \ref{cond:map_condition1} to \ref{cond:map_condition3}, and that the Jacobian matrix of $T$ at $\mathbf{x}$ has a positive determinant for any $\mathbf{x}\in S\setminus \{(0,1)\}$. Then, $T$ satisfies \ref{cond:map_condition4}.
assumptions: Suppose that a map $T:S\to S$ satisfies \ref{cond:map_condition1} to \ref{cond:map_condition3}, and that the Jacobian matrix of $T$ at $\mathbf{x}$ has a positive determinant for any $\mathbf{x}\in S\setminus \{(0,1)\}$.
conclusions: Then, $T$ satisfies \ref{cond:map_condition4}.
nodes.label: lem:criterion_C4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.20
nodes.statement: Let $U\mathrel{\mathop:}= T^{-1}$ and $U(\mathbf{x})=(U_1(\mathbf{x}),U_2(\mathbf{x}))$ for $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)\in S$. By the Inverse Function Theorem (\cref{thm:IFT}), the Jacobian matrix $K$ of $U$ at $\mathbf{x}\in S\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ is given by the inverse of that of $T$. Thus, we have \begin{align*} \frac{\partial U_i}{\partial x_j}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 \end{align*} for any $\mathbf{x}\in S\setminus \{(0,1)\}$. Hence the functions $U_1(x_1,x_2)$ and $U_2(x_1,x_2)$ are nondecreasing on both $x_1$ and $x_2$. Therefore for any two points $(a,b),(c,d)\in S$ of $(a,b)\leq (c,d)$, we have $U_1(a,b) \leq U_1(c,d)$ and $U_2(a,b)\leq U_2(c,d)$ (note that if $(a,b)=(0,1)$ then $(c,d)$ must be $(0,1)$ and we are done).
nodes.statement_short: By the IFT the inverse Jacobian is the inverse of a competitive-sign matrix with positive determinant, hence entrywise nonnegative, so $T^{-1}$ is monotone.

nodes.name: Inverse Jacobian
nodes.statement: Let $U\mathrel{\mathop:}= T^{-1}$ and $U(\mathbf{x})=(U_1(\mathbf{x}),U_2(\mathbf{x}))$ for $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)\in S$. By the Inverse Function Theorem (\cref{thm:IFT}), the Jacobian matrix $K$ of $U$ at $\mathbf{x}\in S\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ is given by the inverse of that of $T$.

nodes.name: Nonnegative partials
nodes.statement: Thus, we have \begin{align*} \frac{\partial U_i}{\partial x_j}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 \end{align*} for any $\mathbf{x}\in S\setminus \{(0,1)\}$. Hence the functions $U_1(x_1,x_2)$ and $U_2(x_1,x_2)$ are nondecreasing on both $x_1$ and $x_2$.

nodes.name: Monotone inverse
nodes.statement: Therefore for any two points $(a,b),(c,d)\in S$ of $(a,b)\leq (c,d)$, we have $U_1(a,b) \leq U_1(c,d)$ and $U_2(a,b)\leq U_2(c,d)$ (note that if $(a,b)=(0,1)$ then $(c,d)$ must be $(0,1)$ and we are done).
